Preface
The Mathematics II Teaching Module for Form II is designed to help teachers prepare and deliver
Competence-Based lessons with a comprehensive understanding of Mathematics concepts,
fostering a deep appreciation for the role of Mathematics in everyday life and its applications in
various fields. This module aims to assist teachers to help learners develop analytical thinking,
problem-solving skills, and project based skills through a structured and progressive learning
approach. This module prescribes on hands-on activities, inquiry-based learning experience,
encouraging learners to explore, experiment, and engage in problem solving reasoning.
This Mathematics II Teaching Module for Form 2 aims to help teachers create a stimulating and
supportive learning environment where learners can develop a profound understanding of
Mathematics. This module will help teachers to guide learners to grow intellectually and
personally by preparing them for professions in Science, Technology, Engineering and
Mathematics (STEM) as well as for higher education by encouraging curiosity, critical thinking,
and practical skills.
It is hoped that this module will inspire learners to explore the fascinating world of Mathematics
and appreciate its significance in shaping the future.
Kelvin Mambwe, (PhD.)
Permanent Secretary- Educational Services

HOW TO USE THIS MODULE
To effectively use this Mathematics II Teaching Module for Form 2:
• Read and familiarise yourself with the module's content, learning activities, and assessment guides.
• Plan your lessons in advance, using the module's suggested teaching and learning activities.
• Use a variety of teaching methods, including demonstrations, discussions, group work, and hands-on activities.
• Encourage active learning by asking open-ended questions, promoting critical thinking, and fostering problem-solving skills.
• Assess learners learning regularly, using the module's suggested assessment strategies and tools.
• Provide feedback and support to learners, helping them to identify areas for improvement and develop their skills.
• Integrate technology into your teaching, using multimedia resources and interactive simulations to enhance learner engagement and understanding.
• Monitor learners progress and adjust your teaching strategies as needed, to ensure that all learners meet the learning objectives
By following these steps, you can effectively use this Mathematics II Teaching Module for Form 2 to support your teaching and promote learning.

INTRODUCTION

Mathematics, as a fundamental STEM subject, which plays an important role in shaping learners' understanding of the natural world. As learners transition from upper primary to secondary education, it is necessary to provide them with an all-inclusive and engaging introduction to Mathematics. Therefore, the Mathematics II Teaching Module for Form 2 is a comprehensive educational resource designed to support the teaching and learning of Mathematics for learners in their first year of secondary education. It covers fundamental concepts and principles of Mathematics, aligning with the 2024 Mathematics syllabus. The module includes topic and subtopic overviews, suggested teaching and learning materials, environment set-up, learning activities, and assessment guides. Additionally, it incorporates teaching methods and strategies like inquiry-based learning, problem-solving activities, group discussions, hands-on activities, multimedia resources, and interactive simulations. The aim is to provide a solid foundation in Mathematics, foster critical thinking and problem-solving skills, and inspire further studies in Mathematics.
SUGGESTED TEACHING AND LEARNING MATERIALS

The study of Mathematics content requires hands-on experiences, visual aids, and interactive resources to strengthen deep understanding and appreciation. To support the teaching and learning of Mathematics II in Form 2, the suggested teaching and learning materials are meant to:
• Enhance learner engagement and motivation in Mathematics
• Develop practical skills and inquiry based thinking
• Promote critical thinking, problem-solving, and analytical skills
• Support differentiated instruction and inclusive learning

The suggested teaching and learning materials are either artificial or natural. By utilising these suggested teaching and learning materials, teachers can create a dynamic and supportive learning environment that promotes academic excellence, creativity, and scientific literacy in Mathematics II for Form 2 learners.
LEARNING ENVIRONMENT SET UP

To create an effective learning environment for teaching and learning Mathematics is important in deepening understanding of the concepts and application in real life context. The learning environment set-up aims to create a safe, inclusive, and engaging space.
• Natural Environment: A natural learning environment is a setting where learners explore and learn naturally, often without explicit instruction or formal teaching, such as in school surroundings

• Artificial Environment (Man-Made): Artificial learning environments are intentionally designed safe spaces, such as classrooms, laboratories, and libraries, designed for formal instruction, hands-on activities, games, and songs

SAFETY IN THE LEARNING ENVIRONMENT

Safety in the learning environment is a requirement in learning Mathematics, as learners are exposed to potential hazards during hands-on activities. Collaboration between teachers, and learners, is important to create a responsible learning environment that promotes scientific inquiry. Guidelines for maintaining a safe learning environment include, risk identification, personal protective equipment, emergency response plans, storage, disposal, and learner responsibilities. Prioritising safety minimises risks, prevents accidents, and ensures a positive learning experience.
TEACHING METHODOLOGY
The effective teaching methodologies in Mathematics II include:
• Conducting projects: Demonstrate key principles and encourage curiosity among learners.
• Collaborative learning: Pair learners to work together, promoting peer-to-peer teaching, discussion, and problem-solving.
• Conceptual learning: Connect mathematical concepts to everyday life, industry, or current events, making learning relevant and meaningful.
• Differentiated instructions: Tailor teaching to meet diverse learning styles, abilities, and interests of different learners.
• Feedback and reflection: Encourage learners to reflect on their learning, providing constructive feedback to guide improvement.
• Inquiry-based learning: Encourage learners to explore, investigate, and discover Mathematical concepts through hands-on activities.
• Integration of technology: Use digital tools, simulations, and visualisations to enhance engagement, understanding, and analysis.
• Problem-based learning: Present real-world problems or case studies or scenarios, requiring learners to apply Mathematical knowledge to develop solutions.
• Project -based learning: Assign open-ended projects, allowing learners to design, conduct, and present research or applications of Mathematical concepts.

LEARNING ACTIVITIES

Learning activities are intentional educational experiences aimed at promoting learning, engagement, and achievement among learners. Facilitated by teachers, they help acquire new knowledge, skills, attitudes, and behaviour change. To create an inclusive environment, teachers should use a "hook" or problem posing or scenario or key question or case studies to introduce new learning activities in an interactive and interesting way.
ICONS USED IN THIS MODULE

This module utilises icons as visual symbols or graphics to represent instructions, enhancing the learning experience for learners. Icons categorise and organise instructions, making navigation easier for teachers.
TIME ALLOCATION

The standard minimum learner-teacher contact time for Mathematics II at secondary school level is 4 hours per week, translating to Six (6) periods with at least two double periods per week. The duration for a single period is 40 minutes. The contact time at Secondary school level is planned in such a way as to give ample time for practical activities.

Class Discussions: Observing learners' participation and engagement in class discussions.
Group Work: Assessing learners' ability to work collaboratively and contribute to group tasks.

TOPIC 4: ALGEBRA
Introduction

Overview: Algebra is a branch of Mathematics that uses letters and symbols to represent numbers and relationships between numbers. It helps us to represent unknown values using letters, write mathematical statements called expressions and equations, find unknown values by solving equations, and describe patterns and real-life situations mathematically. At Form 2 level, algebra builds on the foundational ideas introduced in Form 1 and focuses on helping learners understand and use Algebra as a tool for representing and solving real-life problems. Through learner-centred activities, discussions, and practical tasks, learners develop confidence in manipulating algebraic expressions and applying algebraic methods accurately.
This topic has two sub-topics namely basic processes, and remainder and factor theorems.

Sub-Topic 1: Basic Processes
Introduction

In Form 2, learners are expected to deal with basic processes of Algebra, such as factorising by grouping terms, quadratic expression, and difference of two squares. They are also expected to add, subtract, multiply and divide algebraic fractions, and simplify algebraic fractions using the Lowest Common Multiples (LCM) and factorisation. These basic processes help learners think logically, solve problems, and apply Mathematics to real-life situations. Algebra also provides a foundation for more advanced topics in Mathematics.
Specific Competence: Apply basic processes of Algebra in different contexts
Learning Activity 1: Exploring patterns and relationships in relation to Algebra
Introduction

Algebra is the language we use to describe patterns and relationships in everyday life. From the number of tiles in a growing design, the cost of buying several items, or the distance travelled over time, patterns help us to predict what comes next. Sub-Topic 2: Remainder and Factor Theorems
Introduction

The remainder and factor theorems are important concepts in Algebra because they help learners to understand the relationship between polynomial division and factorisation. These theorems provide a quicker and more meaningful way of determining the remainder when a polynomial is divided by a linear expression, and of checking whether a given expression is a factor of a polynomial. Through this topic, learners develop the ability to simplify polynomial work, factorise cubic expressions, and solve cubic as well as identical cubic equations in an efficient and logical manner.

The study of the remainder and factor theorems also strengthens learners' reasoning, analytical thinking, and problem-solving skills. It enables them to see patterns in algebraic expressions and apply algebraic ideas to both classroom and real-life situations. In this topic, learners will explore the remainder and factor theorems, use them to find quotient and remainder, factorise cubic expressions, solve cubic equations, and use ICT tools to enhance understanding.
Learning Activity 5: Exploring the Remainder and Factor Theorems
Introduction

Instead of performing lengthy polynomial division every time, mathematicians use two powerful tools, namely the Remainder Theorem and the Factor Theorem. These theorems provide efficient shortcuts that connect algebraic division with simple substitution, thereby transforming a complex procedure into a quick calculation. This section explores how and why these theorems work, helping learners move from procedural understanding to conceptual mastery.

Learning Activity 7: Factorising cubic expressions
Introduction

A cubic expression is a polynomial of degree 3, such as 3 + 2 + + where , , and are constants and ≠ 0. Factorising cubic expressions is important because it allows learners to break down complex polynomials into simpler factors, making them easier to solve, analyse, and apply in real-life situations. By factorising cubic expressions, learners can identify roots or zeros of the polynomial, which is essential for solving equations, sketching graphs and understanding the behavior of functions. It also helps learners apply the remainder and factor theorem efficiently and connects directly to higher level topics like Calculus and Algebra, where finding maxima, minima, or point of intersection often requires solving cubic equations. It also prepares learners to model real-world situations in physics, engineering, and economics where relationships are often represented by cubic functions.

Learning Activity 8: Solving cubic equations
Introduction

A cubic equation is a polynomial of degree 3, such as 3 + 2 + + = 0, where , , and are constants and ≠ 0. Solving cubic equations is important because it equips learners with the ability to analyse and model real-world situations that involve non-linear relationships. Unlike linear or quadratic equations, cubic equations can describe more complex patterns, such as growth and decay, volume problems, and physical phenomena where the rate of change is not constant. Mastering cubic equations also helps learners identify roots and intercepts, which is essential for graphing functions, optimising quantities and understanding turning points in higher Mathematics.

In today's digital world, learners are surrounded by technology, from smartphones to computers and interactive learning platforms. Therefore, using ICT tools to teach the Remainder and Factor Theorems transforms abstract algebraic concepts into interactive, visual, and engaging learning experiences. Through tools like GeoGebra, Desmos, and Excel, learners move beyond rote procedures to exploration, verification, and discovery. TOPIC 5: MATRICES
Introduction

Overview: Matrices are an important part of Algebra because they provide an organised way of arranging numbers, symbols, or expressions in rows and columns so that information can be represented, analysed, and manipulated efficiently. They are widely used in Mathematics and in everyday life to organise data such as school records, prices of goods, transport schedules, sports scores, election results, inventories, and timetables. Through Matrices, learners are able to compare related information, perform calculations in an orderly manner, and solve practical problems involving many quantities at once.

The study of Matrices enables learners to develop logical thinking, accuracy, and problem-solving skills. It also helps them to appreciate how Mathematics is used to represent real-life situations in compact and meaningful ways. In practical contexts, matrices can be used in business, science,

Sub-topic: Matrix Operations
Introduction

Matrix operations help learners to organise, analyse, and manipulate data in a systematic way. In everyday life, people use tables and arrangements of numbers to represent information such as prices of goods, examination marks, transport routes, attendance records, and stock lists. Matrices make it possible to handle such information efficiently and to carry out operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and solving equations in a structured way.

Through this sub-topic, learners develop the ability to identify different types of matrices, determine their order, perform operations on them, calculate determinants, find inverses, and apply these ideas in practical contexts. This strengthens logical reasoning, computational skills, and the ability to solve real-life problems using organised numerical information.
Specific Competence: Use matrix operations in day to day activities.
Learning Activity 1: Exploring the concept of matrices
Introduction

Exploring the concept of matrices helps learners understand that numbers and data can be organised in rows and columns for easier interpretation and use. In many real-life situations such as recording test scores, shop prices, classroom attendance, transport charges, and sports results, information is naturally arranged in tabular form. This activity introduces learners to matrices as a mathematical way of representing such organised data.

Problem Posing: A teacher records the Mathematics, English, and Science marks for four learners in a table. The head teacher wants the marks arranged in a simpler form so that they can easily compare the performance of learners in different subjects and carry out calculations later.
Questions
• a) How can the information be arranged using rows and columns?
• b) What makes this arrangement a matrix?
• c) How can the entries in the arrangement be identified?
• d) Why is a matrix useful in such a situation?
Activity 1.1: Research on the concept of matrices
Suggested teaching and learning materials to set up the learning environment
Artificial environment: Textbooks, charts, tables, newspapers, record books, price lists, timetables, and worksheets containing organised data.

Provide them with examples of organised information such as school timetables, class attendance sheets, sports score tables, or shop price lists. Guide learners to observe the arrangement of data into rows and columns and help them relate this arrangement to the concept of a matrix. Ask learners to carry out research on the concept of matrices using computers/phones/tablets and encourage them to discuss where they have seen such arrangements in daily life.

Task: Ask learners in groups to identify examples of organised data from their environment and represent them as matrices. Let them carry out research on the concept of matrices and present their findings to the class.
Skills to be developed: Collaboration, Communication, Critical thinking, Creativity and Innovation, Problem solving, and Research skills.
Activity 1.2: Arranging data into matrices
Suggested teaching and learning materials to set up the learning environment
Artificial environment: Manila papers, markers, counters, and worksheets with tables of data.

What to Do: Present learners with practical information such as prices of mealie meal, sugar, and cooking oil in different shops, or scores obtained by teams in a sports competition. Guide them to arrange the data into rows and columns and identify each entry by position. Help learners understand that each number has a location described by its row and column.
Task: Let learners in groups arrange given sets of information into matrices and identify selected entries using row and column positions. Let them present their work to the class.

Content Tip: Help learners understand that a matrix is not just any table, but a structured mathematical arrangement of entries in rows and columns. Emphasise that position matters, and that each entry can be identified by its location. Encourage learners to move from practical tables to symbolic notation gradually.

Learning Activity 2: Identifying different types of matrices (row, column, square, zero, rectangular, equal, diagonal, identity)
Introduction

Identifying different types of matrices helps learners classify matrices according to their structure. This enables them to recognise similarities and differences between matrices and to prepare for later operations. Learners come to understand that matrices may be row matrices, column matrices, square matrices, rectangular matrices, zero matrices, diagonal matrices, equal matrices, or identity matrices depending on their arrangement and entries.

Problem Posing: A school has different records: one contains a single row of transport costs, another contains a single column of attendance numbers, another records test marks in a square arrangement, and another has only zeros because no books have yet been issued from the library. The teacher wants learners to classify these matrices correctly and it happens that you are among these learners. How can these matrices be grouped according to their form?

Suggested teaching and learning materials to set up the learning environment
Artificial environment: Flash cards with matrices, and worksheets.

Introduction

Stating the order of a matrix helps learners describe its size accurately and prepares them for performing Matrix operations correctly. Since many matrix operations depend on the order of the matrices involved, learners need to know how to count rows and columns correctly. This activity strengthens attention to detail and mathematical precision.

Problem Posing: A learner writes a matrix from a classroom attendance record but is unsure of its order. The class now wants to determine the correct way of its order. As a member of the class, help the class to state the correct order.

Artificial environment: Worksheets, manila papers, markers, and charts with examples of matrices of different sizes.

Learning Activity 4: Transposing matrices
Introduction

Transposing Matrices helps learners understand that the arrangement of entries in a Matrix can be changed systematically by interchanging rows and columns. This activity develops the ability of learners to observe structure and relationships within Matrices. It also helps them to appreciate how a Matrix can be represented in a different but related form without changing the actual entries. In practical situations, transposition can be used when reorganising information such as changing data recorded by days and subjects into subjects and days, or changing lists of items and prices into prices and items for easier comparison and analysis.

Problem Posing: A class teacher records the marks of learners in three subjects using a matrix in which the rows represent learners and the columns represent subjects. The deputy head teacher wants the same information rearranged so that the rows represent subjects and the columns represent learners.
Questions
• a) How can the original Matrix be changed to suit the new arrangement?
• b) What happens to the rows and columns during the change?

Activity 4.1: Investigating the transpose of a Matrix
Suggested teaching and learning materials to set up the learning environment
• Artificial environment: Manila papers, markers, flash cards with Matrices, and charts showing rows and columns clearly.

• Technological environment: Projector for displaying matrix examples and animations of row-column interchange, computer/tablet/phone with software such as Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, and MATLAB or Python (with NumPy) for rotating rows and columns.

What to do: Put learners in small manageable groups of mixed abilities. Start with the problem posed. Provide each group with simple matrices written on flash cards. Guide learners to copy each Matrix and then interchange the rows and columns carefully. Ask learners to use computer/phone/tablet with software to rotate rows and columns and present their findings to the class using a projector for displaying animations. Let them compare the original Matrix with the new one and describe what has changed. Offer help where necessary as learners discuss the meaning of transposition and identify how entries move from one position to another.

Task: Ask learners in groups to find the transpose of given matrices and present their findings to the class. Let them explain how the rows of the original Matrix become the columns of the new matrix.

Content Tip: Help learners understand that to transpose a matrix means to interchange rows and columns. Emphasise that the first row of the original Matrix becomes the first column of the transpose, the second row becomes the second column, and so on. Let learners practice with small matrices first before moving to larger ones. Encourage them to trace the movement of entries carefully so that they develop confidence and accuracy.
Skills to be developed: Collaboration, Communication, Critical thinking, and Digital literacy.
Conceptualisation: Ensure that the concept of the transpose of a matrix comes out clearly. Give brief notes and examples showing how rows become columns and columns become rows.

Learning Activity 5: Performing basic matrix operations on Matrices (addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication and multiplication up to order × )
Introduction

Performing basic Matrix operations helps learners use matrices in a practical and meaningful way. Once learners know how Matrices are formed and classified, they should be able to add, subtract, and multiply matrices by a scalar. They should also begin to understand Matrix multiplication as a structured operation based on rows and columns. These operations allow learners to combine and compare organised data, making Matrices useful in practical situations such as shop records, transport fare tables, school results, budgets, and inventories.

Through this activity, learners strengthen computational accuracy, logical thinking, and problemsolving skills. They also begin to appreciate the conditions under which certain operations are possible, especially that matrices must have the same order for addition and subtraction to be performed.

Problem Posing: Two shops record the number of exercise books, pens, and rulers sold during two days. A teacher wants to combine the sales records, compare the difference in sales, and also calculate how the sales would look if every value were doubled during a promotion. In another case, the teacher wants learners to see how rows and columns can be used to multiply matrices in practical situations.
Question
How can you help the teacher combine the sales records, compare differences in sales, and calculate how the sales would look if the values doubled during a promotion?

Learning Activity 7: Using the concept of determinants to find the inverse of a × and × Matrix
Introduction

Finding inverse matrices using determinants helps learners understand how a square matrix can be reversed in a way that is similar to finding the reciprocal of a number. The inverse of a matrix is important in solving matrix equations and systems of linear equations. Through this activity, learners discover that not every square matrix has an inverse, and that the determinant helps to decide whether the inverse exists.

This activity strengthens the computational ability of learners, attention to detail, and reasoning. It also helps them connect earlier concepts such as square matrices, determinants, and identity matrices. By working with inverse matrices, learners see how different areas of algebra come together to solve practical problems in an organised way.

Problem Posing: A group of learners is given a matrix representing information from a real-life situation in which they were required to calculate the determinant and make decisions. As they begin the task, they discover that some matrices can be inverted while others cannot. The teacher challenges them to investigate the condition that determines whether a matrix has an inverse and to explain how the inverse can be found and used in solving the problem. Under what condition does the given matrix have an inverse?

Introduction

Proving matrix properties helps learners to move beyond computation and develop a deeper understanding of how matrices behave under different operations. These properties help learners to work more confidently and accurately when adding, subtracting, or multiplying matrices.

This activity also strengthens logical thinking, reasoning, and the ability to justify mathematical statements. By proving matrix properties, learners begin to appreciate that mathematics is not only about getting answers but also about explaining why methods work. Introduction

Solving systems of linear equations using matrices helps learners apply matrix concepts to practical problem solving. Many real-life situations involve two or more unknown quantities that must be determined simultaneously. Such situations arise in business, farming, transport, science, and education. Matrices provide a clear and organised method for representing and solving such systems.

Through this activity, learners connect earlier ideas such as matrix formation, determinants, inverse matrices, and matrix operations. This strengthens their understanding of algebra as a whole and helps them appreciate the usefulness of matrices in solving problems involving several unknowns at the same time. Learners also develop reasoning, interpretation, and problem-solving skills.

Introduction

Overview: Variation in Mathematics describes the relationship between two quantities and how a change in one quantity affects the other. It helps learners understand how variables are connected and how mathematical models can represent real-life situations. In this topic, learners explore different types of relationships between variables such direct, inverse, joint, and partial variations. They learn how to express these relationships using mathematical equations, tables and graphs. For example, when two quantities increase or decrease together at a constant rate, they are said to vary directly. When one quantity increases while the other decreases, they vary inversely. Understanding variation helps learners apply Mathematics to real-life situations such as, speed and time relationships, cost and quantity relationships, pressure and volume in science, and other proportional relationships.
Through this topic, learners develop skills in algebraic thinking, problem-solving, graph interpretation, and mathematical communication.

Terms /Words/Vocabulary:

Variation: A relationship between two or more variables where a change in one affects the other. Variable: A symbol (usually a letter) that represents a quantity that can change. Constant of Variation: A fixed number that relates the variables in a variation equation. Direct Variation: When two quantities increase or decrease together in the same proportion. Inverse Variation: When one quantity increases while the other decreases proportionally. Joint Variation: When one variable varies directly with two or more variables. Partial Variation: A relationship between variables where one variable changes partly in direct proportion to another variable and partly as a constant (fixed amount). Proportional Relationships: A relationship where two quantities maintain a constant ratio. Equation of Variation: A mathematical expression that represents the relationship between variables. Graph of Variation: A visual representation of the relationship between variables on a coordinate plane.
Sub-topic: Types of Variation
Introduction

Types of variation help learners understand how quantities change in relation to each other. This knowledge is important for solving practical problems in everyday life and for developing strong mathematical skills. The main types of variation are direct, inverse, joint, and partial variations. These are widely used in real-life situations such as, wages and hours worked, speed and travel time, number of workers and time taken to complete a job, force in physics, intensity of light, and many others.
Specific Competence: Apply the concept of variation in daily contexts.

Learning Activity 2: Exploring the concept of Variation.
Introduction

Exploring the concept of variation enables learners to understand how different quantities change in relation to each other in real-life situations. Through hands on activities such as investigating distance and time, number of workers and time taken to complete a task, shadow length and time of day, water flow and time, learners observe and analyse patterns of change.
Problem Posing: A group of learners in a school garden observe the growth of a plant. Each week they measure the height of a plant. Assuming that all the necessary conditions are present.
Questions
• (a) How does the height of the plant vary with time?
• (b) Does the plant grow by the same amount every week?
• (c) Can you predict the plant's height after several weeks?

Learning Activity 3: Identifying types of Variations (Direct, Inverse, Joint, and Partial).
Introduction

At this level, four types of variations are covered, namely, direct variation, which shows proportional increase or decrease, Inverse variation, which shows opposite change between variables, Joint variation, which involves dependence on multipole variables, and Partial variation, which combines a constant value with a varying component. Understanding types of variation helps learners to recognise how quantities relate in real-life situations. Through investigation, experimentation, and real-world simulations learners can understand how variables relate, and that helps us to predict outcomes, model-real-world situations, and solve practical problems in fields such as science, economics, and engineering.

Problem Posing: Imagine you are planning a school trip. The cost per learner decreases as more learners join the trip, but the total cost increases depending on the number of days and activities planned. Why does the relationship between these quantities change?

Suggested teaching and learning materials to set up learning environment.

• 4. Solve for the variable in question.

State the type of variation in each of the following situations:
• (a) The cost of fuel varies with the number of litres bought.
• (b) The time taken to finish a job varies with the number of workers.
• (c) The volume of a box varies with its length and width.
• (d) A taxi fare includes a fixed charge plus a cost depending on a distance travelled.

A small factory produces bottled juice. The number of bottles produced varies directly with the number of hours the machine operates. When the machine runs for 4 hours, it produces 320 bottles of juice.
• (a) Write an equation that relates the number of bottles B to the number of hours h,
• (b) How many bottles will be produced in 7 hours?
• (c) How long will it take to produce 1,200 bottles of juice?
A group of workers is hired to paint a school building. The time required to complete the work varies inversely with the number of workers. It takes 12 days for 6 workers to finish the job.
• (a) Write the inverse variation equation relating time t and the number of workers w,
• (b) How long will the job take if 9 workers are hired?
• (c) How many workers are needed to finish the job in 4 days?

Chaona is a farmer in Kabwe rural and supplies maize to a milling company that produces mealie meal for sale in nearby markets including Lusaka and Ndola. She records production, transportation and milling costs using mathematical models to help her plan operations efficiently.

The transport manager models the cost per tonne using the expression \frac{2x}{x^2-9} + \frac{3}{x+3} - \frac{1}{x-3}, where x represents the fuel adjustment factor.
